concepts.title: Cosine Series
concepts.one_liner: Fourier series can be expressed as sums of cosine functions, representing a function through its harmonic components.
concepts.content:
Fourier series can be written as sums of different sets of harmonic functions. For instance, using cosine functions we can describe the ramp function as:
$$\frac{1}{2} t =  \frac{\pi}{4}  - \frac{2}{\pi} \cos (t) - \frac{2}{3^2 \pi}  \cos (3t) - \frac{2}{5^2 \pi}  \cos (5t) - ...$$
The cosine and sine series of the same function are only equal in the interval $t \in (0, \pi)$, and result in different periodic extensions outside that interval.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing functions using only cosine terms is useful for analyzing signals with even symmetry or for creating specific periodic extensions of a function defined on a finite interval.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier series can be constructed using a set of harmonic cosine functions.
- The cosine series and sine series of a function generally differ outside the interval $(0, \pi)$.

concepts.title: Continuous Time Sine Wave
concepts.one_liner: The continuous time sine wave is defined by its amplitude, frequency, and phase.
concepts.content:
The **continuous time sine wave** is
$$s\left(t\right) = A \sin\left(w ~t - \theta \right)$$
where $A$ is the **amplitude**, $w$ is the **frequency**, and $\theta$ is the **phase**. The wave signal is periodic with a period $T=2 \pi / w$.

concepts.recap_md:

concepts.title: Discrete Time Sine Wave
concepts.one_liner: A discrete time sine wave is a sampled version of a sinusoid that is periodic only for specific rational frequencies.
concepts.content:
In discrete time, the **discrete time sine wave** is defined as:
$$s\left[n\right] = A \sin\left(w ~n  - \theta \right)$$
Note that the discrete sine wave will not be periodic for any arbitrary value of $w$. A discrete signal $\ell\left[n\right]$ is periodic if there exists $T \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\ell\left[n\right] = \ell\left[n+mT\right]$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$. For the discrete sine (and cosine) wave to be periodic, the frequency must be $w = 2 \pi K / N$ for $K,N \in \mathbb{N}$. If $K/N$ is an irreducible fraction, then the period of the wave will be $T = N$ samples.

Although $\theta$ can have any value, we often consider $\theta=0$ and $\theta = \pi/2$, which correspond to the sine and cosine waves, respectively. To make the periodicity explicit, we use the form:
$$s_k\left[n\right] = \sin\left( \frac{2 \pi}{N} \, k \, n \right)$$
$$c_k\left[n\right] = \cos\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N} \,k\,n \right)$$
This notation is useful for signals with period $N$ or finite support of length $N$ where $n \in [0, N-1]$. Here, $k \in [1, N/2]$ denotes the frequency. Note that if $k=0$, then $s[n] = 0$ and $c[n]=1$. Also, $c_{N-k} = c_k$ and $s_{N-k} = -s_k$, meaning frequencies $k > N/2$ mirror those in the interval $[1, N/2]$.

(see figure: Sine and cosine waves with $A=1$ and $N=20$. Each row corresponds to $k=1$, $k=2$ and $k=3$. Note that for $k=3$ the waves oscillates three times in the interval $\left[0,N-1\right)$, but the samples in each oscillation are not identical, and it is only truly periodic once every $N$ samples. This is because $3/20$ is an irreducible fraction.]

concepts.recap_md:
- Periodicity requires the frequency $w$ to be a rational multiple of $2\pi$.
- The frequency $k$ represents the number of cycles within a support region of length $N$.

concepts.title: Sines and Cosines in 2D
concepts.one_liner: Two-dimensional discrete sine and cosine waves are defined by spatial frequencies that determine the rate of change along two dimensions.
concepts.content:
The analysis of discrete waves can be extended to two dimensions (2D). In 2D, the discrete sine and cosine waves are defined as:
$$s_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = A \sin \left(2 \pi \left( \frac{u\,n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
$$c_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = A \cos \left(2 \pi \left( \frac{u\,n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
where $A$ is the amplitude and $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial frequencies. These frequencies define how fast or slow the waves change along the spatial dimensions $n$ and $m$.

(see figure: 2D sine waves with $N=M=20$. The frequency values are (a) $u=2, v=0$; (b) $u=3, v=1$; (c) $u=7,v=-5$.)
concepts.motivation_md: 2D sinusoids are the basis for image processing and spatial frequency analysis, allowing images to be decomposed into directional patterns.
concepts.recap_md:
- 2D waves use two spatial frequencies, $u$ and $v$, to define oscillations across a grid.
- The indices $n$ and $m$ represent spatial coordinates in the discrete 2D plane.

concepts.title: Complex Exponential Wave
concepts.one_liner: The complex exponential wave is a fundamental signal relating real and imaginary components through Euler's formula.
concepts.content:
The complex exponential wave is defined as:
$$e_{u}\left[n\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j   \frac{u\, n}{N}   \right)$$
Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula: $\exp(ja) = \cos(a) + j\sin(a)$. As $n$ goes from 0 to $N-1$, the function rotates along the complex circle of unit magnitude. In a plot of the real component ($x$-axis) versus the imaginary component ($y$-axis), this rotation becomes visible.

concepts.recap_md:

- Represents a rotation around the unit circle in the complex plane as $n$ increases.

concepts.title: Euler's Formula
concepts.one_liner: Euler's formula relates complex exponentials to trigonometric functions: $\exp(ja) = \cos(a) + j\sin(a)$.
concepts.content:
Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's formula:
$$\exp \left(j a\right) = \cos (a) + j \sin (a)$$ 
This formula provides the link between circular motion in the complex plane and oscillatory trigonometric functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Euler's formula is the bridge between trigonometry and complex analysis, allowing for much easier manipulation of periodic signals.
concepts.recap_md:
- Connects complex exponentials to sine and cosine functions.
- Fundamental for representing signals in the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Separability of Complex Exponentials
concepts.one_liner: Two-dimensional complex exponentials are separable, meaning they can be expressed as the product of two one-dimensional signals.
concepts.content:
In 2D, the complex exponential wave is defined as:
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j \left(  \frac{u\, n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
where $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial frequencies. A key property is that complex exponentials in 2D are separable. This means they can be written as the product of two 1D signals:
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right]   = e_{u}\left[n\right] e_{v}\left[m\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Separability allows complex 2D operations, like the Fourier Transform, to be computed as a series of simpler 1D operations, greatly improving computational efficiency.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 2D complex exponential is the product of a horizontal and a vertical 1D complex exponential.
- This property simplifies the analysis and processing of 2D signals like images.

concepts.title: Orthogonality of Complex Exponentials
concepts.one_liner: Complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis, allowing any finite discrete signal to be decomposed into a linear combination of them.
concepts.content:
A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For images of size $N \times M$, the inner product is given by:
$$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$
Therefore, any finite length discrete image can be decomposed as a linear combination of complex exponentials.
concepts.motivation_md: Orthogonality ensures that each frequency component in a signal can be analyzed independently, which is the theoretical foundation of the Fourier Transform.
concepts.recap_md:
- Complex exponentials serve as an orthogonal basis for finite discrete signals.
- Any discrete image can be represented as a sum of these basis functions.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of the Delta Distribution
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the delta function $\delta \left[n,m \right]$ is equal to 1.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform of the delta function $\delta \left[n,m \right]$ is $$\mathcal{F} \left\{ \delta \left[n,m \right] \right\} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \delta \left[n,m \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} = 1$$ where the Fourier transform of the delta signal is 1: $$\delta \left[n,m \right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 1$$ If we think in terms of the inverse Fourier transform, this means that if we sum all the complex exponentials with a coefficient of 1, then all the values will cancel but the one at the origin, which results in a delta function: $$\delta \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{u=-N/2}^{N/2} \sum_{v=-M/2}^{M/2} \exp{ \left(2\pi j \left(\frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right) }$$
concepts.motivation_md: The delta function is the simplest possible signal in the spatial domain, representing a single point. Understanding its Fourier transform—which is a constant—establishes the fundamental relationship between localization in space and spread in frequency.
concepts.recap_md: - The Fourier transform of a discrete delta function $\delta[n,m]$ is a constant value of 1.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of Real and Even Signals
concepts.one_liner: Real and even input signals result in Fourier transforms that are also real and even.
concepts.content: From the Fourier transform equation, one can show that real and even input signals transform to real and even outputs. For signals symmetric about the spatial origin, the imaginary component of the Fourier transform happens to be zero. In such cases, the magnitude of the Fourier transform is simply the absolute value of the real component. Additionally, if an image is separable (it can be written as the product of two 1D signals), its DFT is also the product of 1D DFTs.
concepts.motivation_md: Symmetry in the spatial domain simplifies calculations in the frequency domain. Recognizing real and even signals allows us to ignore the imaginary part of the transform, making analysis more efficient.
concepts.recap_md: - Real and even signals produce real and even Fourier transforms.

concepts.title: 2D Box Function and its DFT
concepts.one_liner: The 2D DFT of a box function is the product of two 1D DFTs due to its separability.
concepts.content: A 2D box is a separable function and can be written as the product of two box functions: $\text{box}_{L_n, L_m} \left[n,m\right] = \text{box}_{L_n} \left[n\right] \text{box}_{L_m}\left[m\right]$. Because of this property, the DFT is also the product of the two 1D DFTs: $$\text{Box}_{L_n, L_m} \left[ u,v \right] = \text{Box}_{L_n} \left[ u\right] \text{Box}_{L_m} \left[ v\right].$$ As the support of the image in one domain gets larger, the magnitude in the other domain becomes more localized.
concepts.motivation_md: The 2D box function is a standard model for rectangular apertures or simple filters. Leveraging its separability simplifies the computation of its 2D Fourier transform into two 1D problems.
concepts.recap_md: - A 2D box function is separable into the product of two 1D box functions.

concepts.title: Box Function Definition
concepts.one_liner: The box function is defined as 1 inside a specific interval $[-L, L]$ and 0 elsewhere.
concepts.content: The box function is defined as follows: $$\text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] = \begin{cases} 1 & \quad \text{if } -L \leq n \leq L \\ 0 & \quad \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$ The box function takes values of 1 inside the interval $\left[ -L,L \right]$ and it is 0 outside. The duration of the box is $2L+1$. It is useful to think of the box function as a finite length signal of length $N$ and to visualize its periodic extension outside of that interval. concepts.title: Derivation of the DFT of the Box Function
concepts.one_liner: The DFT of a box function is derived using the geometric series formula to arrive at a ratio of sine functions.
concepts.content: To compute the DFT of the finite length box function with length $N$, we use the DFT definition and the periodic nature of the terms: $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{F} \left\{ \text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] \right\} &= \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \, \text{box}_{L} \left[n \right] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)} \\ &= \sum_{n=-L}^{L} \, \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)} \end{aligned}$$ Using the equation for the sum of a geometric series $\sum_{n=-L}^{L} a^n = \frac{a^{-(2L+1)/2}-a^{(2L+1)/2}}{a^{-1/2}-a^{1/2}}$ with $a = \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)}$, we can write the sum as: $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{n=-L}^{L} \, \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \frac{u\, n}{N} \right)} &= \frac{\exp{ \left( \pi j \frac{u(2L+1)}{N} \right)} - \exp{ \left( -\pi j \frac{u(2L+1)}{N} \right)}} {\exp{ \left( \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)} - \exp{ \left( - \pi j \frac{u}{N} \right)} } \\ &= \frac{\sin \left( \pi u(2L+1)/N \right)}{\sin \left( \pi u/N \right)} \end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Shift Property (Translation in Space)
concepts.one_liner: Translating a signal in the spatial domain results in multiplying its Fourier transform by a complex exponential.
concepts.content:
A shift corresponds to a translation in space. Translating a signal $\ell[n,m]$ in the spatial domain by $(n_0, m_0)$ pixels results in multiplying its Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$ by a complex exponential. Specifically, for an image with period $N,M$, the Fourier transform of the displaced image $\ell[n-n_0,m-m_0]$ is given by:

$$\begin{split} \mathcal{F} \{ \ell[n-n_0,m-m_0] \} &= \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell[n-n_0,m-m_0] \exp{ \left( -2
\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n}{N} + \frac{v\, m}{M} \right) \right)} \\ &= \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell[n,m] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, (n+n_0)}{N} + \frac{v\, (m+m_0)}{M} \right) \right)} \\ &= \mathscr{L}[u,v] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)} \end{split}$$

Because the signal $\ell$ and the complex exponentials have period $N,M$, the sum indices can be changed over any range of size $N \times M$ samples. In practice, this property is strictly true only for a circular shift, where pixels disappearing on one boundary reappear on the opposite side. For standard translations, such as those caused by camera motion, boundary artifacts and new pixels appearing mean the shift property is only an approximation.
concepts.motivation_md: The shift property allows us to understand how spatial movement affects the frequency domain. It is fundamental for tasks like motion estimation, image registration, and understanding the phase information of the Fourier transform.
concepts.recap_md:
- A spatial translation by $(n_0, m_0)$ results in a phase shift in the frequency domain.
- The Fourier transform is multiplied by $\exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u\, n_0}{N} + \frac{v\, m_0}{M} \right) \right)}$.

concepts.title: Modulation Property (Translation in Frequency)
concepts.one_liner: Multiplying an image by a complex exponential translates its Fourier transform, a process known as modulation.
concepts.content:
If an image is multiplied by a complex exponential, its Fourier transform is translated. This is known as the modulation property:

$$\ell[n,m] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)} \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}[u-u_0,v-v_0]$$

This relationship can be proven using the dual convolution property. Because the resulting signal is not real, its Fourier Transform does not exhibit symmetries around $u,v=0$. A related relationship involving a cosine wave is:

$$\ell[n,m] \cos{ \left( 2\pi j \left( \frac{u_0\, n}{N} + \frac{v_0\, m}{M} \right) \right)} \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}[u-u_0,v-v_0] + \mathscr{L}[u+u_0,v+v_0]$$

Multiplying a signal by a wave is called signal modulation, a fundamental operation in communications and image analysis. (see figure: Modulation in space. concepts.title: Fourier Transform for Continuous Signals
concepts.one_liner: The continuous Fourier transform is used for infinite length signals and operations like derivatives that are best defined in the continuous domain.
concepts.content:
The continuous domain is convenient for functions and operations not defined in the discrete domain, such as the derivative operator or the Gaussian distribution. For infinite length signals in the continuous domain, the Fourier transform is defined as:

$$\mathscr{L}(w) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ell(t) \exp{ \left( - j w t \right)} \, dt$$

where $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a continuous function of frequency $w$ (in radians). The inverse Fourier transform is given by:

$$\ell(t) = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{ \left( j w t \right) } \, dw$$

Most properties of the DFT apply to the continuous domain by replacing sums with integrals.

- It is particularly useful for operations like differentiation and continuous distributions like the Gaussian.
- Frequency $w$ is a continuous variable in radians.

concepts.one_liner: Convolution between two continuous signals is defined by an integral across the spatial variables.

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform for infinite length discrete signals results in a continuous, periodic frequency representation.
concepts.content:
For discrete signals with infinite length, the Fourier transform sum becomes infinite. By replacing $w = 2 \pi u / N$, the transform is written as:
$$\mathscr{L}(w) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell[n] \exp{(- j w n)}$$
In this case, the frequency $w$ is a continuous variable, and the Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}(w)$ is a periodic function with period $2 \pi$. The inverse Fourier transform is:
$$\ell[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{2 \pi} \mathscr{L}(w) \exp{(j w n)} d w$$
where the integration is performed over a single period.

- The transform for infinite discrete signals results in a continuous and $2\pi$-periodic frequency domain.
- The inverse transform requires integration over only one period of the frequency spectrum.

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of an image can be expressed in polar form as the product of an amplitude component and an exponential phase component.

$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  = A \left[u,v \right] \, \exp{\left( j\, \theta\left[u,v \right]  \right)}$$
where $A \left[u,v \right] = \left| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]  \right|$ and $\theta \left[u,v \right] = \angle  \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$.

concepts.title: Interpretation of Fourier Amplitude and Phase

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: Location information typically resides in the phase, while intensity scaling and signal strength reside in the magnitude.
concepts.content:
Decomposing the Fourier transform of a signal into its amplitude and phase is a useful image representation. In terms of the inverse Fourier transform, $A \left[u,v \right]$ gives the strength of the weight for each complex exponential, while the phase $\theta \left[u,v \right]$ translates the complex exponential. 

The phase carries information about where image contours are by specifying how the phases of the sinusoids must line up to create observed edges. Translating an image in space only modifies the phase of its Fourier transform. In short, location information goes into the phase while intensity scaling goes into the magnitude.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the distinct roles of amplitude and phase helps in tasks like image registration, edge detection, and understanding how spatial shifts affect frequency data.

concepts.title: Phase Dominance in Natural Images

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: In many natural images, the phase component dominates the visual appearance and determines the location of edges and colors.
concepts.content:
The appearance of natural images is often dominated by the phase of their Fourier transform. This is demonstrated by experiments swapping the phases and amplitudes of two different images.

(see figure: Swapping the amplitude and the phase of the Fourier Transform of two images. Each color channel is processed in the same way.)

When an image is reconstructed using the amplitude of one image and the phase of another, the resulting image's appearance mostly resembles the source of the phase. For example, an image built with the phase of a stop sign will look like a stop sign even if the amplitude comes from a different image. The phase signal determines where the edges and colors are located, though final colors may be altered if amplitudes change.

concepts.title: DFT Magnitude Decay in Natural Images

position.section_title: Fourier Analysis as an Image Representation

concepts.one_liner: The magnitude of the DFT for natural images typically peaks at the origin and decays inversely proportional to radial frequency.
concepts.content: A remarkable property of natural images is that the magnitude of their DFT generally has its maximum at the origin and decays inversely proportional to the radial frequency. The magnitude of the DFT of natural images is quite similar across different scenes and can be approximated by $A \left[u,v \right] = a/ (u^2+v^2)^b$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. This typical structure has been used as a prior for many tasks such as image denoising.

concepts.title: Linearity of the Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform and its inverse are linear transformations.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform and its inverse are linear transformations:
$$\alpha \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] + \beta \ell_2 \left[ n,m \right]  
\xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} 
\alpha \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] + \beta \mathscr{L}_2 \left[ u,v \right]$$
where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complex numbers. This property can be easily proven from the definition of the DFT.
concepts.motivation_md: Linearity allows us to compute the Fourier transform of a complex signal by breaking it down into a weighted sum of simpler components, facilitating easier analysis and processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT of a linear combination of signals is the same linear combination of their individual DFTs.
- This property applies to both the forward and inverse Fourier transforms.

- The 2D DFT of a separable signal is the product of the 1D DFTs of its components.

concepts.title: Parseval's Theorem
concepts.one_liner: Parseval's theorem states that the dot product and norm of signals are preserved after a Fourier basis change.
concepts.content:
### Parseval's Theorem

As the DFT is a change of basis, the dot product between two signals and the norm of a vector is preserved (up to a constant factor) after the basis change. This is stated by Parseval's theorem:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \ell_1 \left[n,m \right] \ell_2^* \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v \right] \mathscr{L}_2^* \left[u,v \right]$$
In particular, if $\ell_1=\ell_2$ this reduces to the **Plancherel theorem**:
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \ell\left[n,m \right] \|^2 = \frac{1}{NM}\sum_{u=0}^{N-1} \sum_{v=0}^{M-1} \,  \| \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right] \|^2$$
This relationship is important because it tells us that the energy of a signal can be computed as the sum of the squared magnitude of the values of its Fourier transform.
concepts.motivation_md: Parseval's theorem ensures that the total energy of a signal remains consistent whether it is measured in the spatial domain or the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md:
- The DFT preserves the dot product and norm of signals up to a constant factor $1/NM$.
- The energy of a signal can be computed by summing the squared magnitudes in either the spatial or frequency domain.

concepts.title: Convolution Property of the DFT
concepts.one_liner: The operation of a convolution in the spatial domain corresponds to multiplication in the Fourier domain.
concepts.content:
### Convolution

Consider a signal $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$ that is the result of applying (circular) convolution of two signals, $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$, both of size $N \times M$: $$\ell_{\texttt{out}}= \ell_1 \circ \ell_2$$

If we take the Fourier transform of both sides and use the definition of the Fourier transform, we obtain:
$$\begin{split}
\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] & =  \mathcal{F}  \left\{ \ell_1 \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \right\} \\
& =  
\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}  \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} 
\left\{
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1} 
\ell_1 \left[n-k, m-l \right] \ell_2 \left[k,l \right]
\right\}
\exp \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{nu}{N} + \frac{mv}{M} \right) \right)
\end{split}$$
In these sums, the finite signal $\ell_1 \left[n, m \right]$ is extended periodically. Changing the dummy variables ($n' = n - k$ and $m' = m - l$) and recognizing the DFT of $x[n,m]$ using circular boundary conditions, we find:
$$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \sum_{l=0}^{M-1}  \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \exp{ \left(-2 \pi j \left(\frac{ku}{N}+\frac{lv}{M} \right ) \right)} \ell_2 \left[k,l\right]$$
Performing the final DFT gives the desired result:
$$\mathscr{L}_{\texttt{out}}\left[u,v\right] = \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$

Thus, the operation of a convolution, in the Fourier domain, is just a multiplication of the Fourier transform of each term:
$$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \circ_{N,M} \ell_2 \left[n,m\right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Convolution is computationally expensive in the spatial domain. This property allows us to perform convolution much faster by multiplying in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md:
- Spatial circular convolution corresponds to point-wise multiplication in the frequency domain.
- This relationship is fundamental for efficient linear filtering of images.

concepts.title: Fourier Bases as Eigenfunctions of LSI Systems
concepts.one_liner: Fourier bases are the eigenfunctions of all space-invariant linear operators.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform lets us characterize images by their spatial frequency content. It's also the natural domain in which to analyze space-invariant linear processes, because the Fourier bases are the eigenfunctions of all space-invariant linear operators. In other words, if you apply any linear, space-invariant operator to a complex exponential, the result is always a complex exponential of that same frequency, though generally with a different amplitude and phase.
concepts.motivation_md: This property explains why the Fourier transform is so powerful for LSI systems: it diagonalizes the operator, turning complex convolutions into simple scalar multiplications.
concepts.recap_md:
- Fourier bases are eigenfunctions of linear space-invariant (LSI) systems.
- Applying an LSI operator to a complex exponential preserves its frequency, only altering amplitude and phase.

concepts.title: Dual Convolution Property (Product in Space)
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of the product of two images is the circular convolution of their individual DFTs.
concepts.content:
### Dual Convolution

Another common operation when working with images is to compute products between images. For instance, this occurs when applying a mask to an image, which corresponds to multiplying the image by a mask that has zeros in the pixels to be excluded.

It turns out that the Fourier transform of the product of two images is the (circular) convolution of their DFTs:

$$\ell_1 \left[n,m\right] \ell_2 \left[n,m\right] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \frac{1}{NM} \mathscr{L}_1 \left[u,v\right] \circ \mathscr{L}_2 \left[u,v\right]$$
concepts.motivation_md: This property is the dual of the convolution theorem; it explains how point-wise operations like masking or windowing affect the frequency spectrum of a signal.
concepts.recap_md:
- Point-wise multiplication in the spatial domain corresponds to circular convolution in the frequency domain.
- The resulting frequency convolution is scaled by a factor of $1/NM$.

concepts.title: Spatial Frequency

The Fourier transform lets us describe a signal as a sum of complex exponentials, each of a different spatial frequency.

concepts.title: Image Transforms
concepts.one_liner: Image transforms convert pixel data into alternative representations to reveal properties useful for vision tasks.
concepts.content: Sometimes it is useful to transform image pixels into another representation that might reveal image properties useful for solving vision tasks. Linear image transforms with the form $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ can be thought of as a way of changing the initial pixels representation of $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ into a different intermediate representation $\mathbf{x}$. This representation is especially interesting when it can be inverted so that the original pixels can be recovered as $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}= \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{x}$. The Fourier transform is one of those representations. A useful representation $\mathbf{x}$ should have interesting properties not immediately available in the original pixels.
concepts.motivation_md: Transforms allow us to process images in domains where certain features are more easily isolated or where operations like compression and filtering are more computationally efficient.
concepts.recap_md: - They map pixel data to a new mathematical space to highlight specific properties. - Invertible transforms allow for the perfect reconstruction of the original image from the transformed representation.

concepts.title: Fourier Series
concepts.one_liner: A Fourier series represents a periodic signal as an infinite sum of harmonically related trigonometric functions.
concepts.content: In 1822, Joseph Fourier showed that any periodic signal could be written as an infinite sum of trigonometric functions (cosine and sine). Fourier showed that any function $\ell(t)$ defined in the interval $t \in (0,\pi)$ could be expressed as an infinite linear combination of harmonically related sinusoids: $$\ell(t) = a_1 \sin (t) + a_2 \sin (2t) + a_3 \sin (3t) + ...$$ The coefficients $a_n$ are computed as the area of the curve $\ell(t) \sin (nt)$, specifically: $$a_n = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi  \ell(t) \sin (nt) dt$$ The resulting sum is a periodic function with period $2\pi$ and is anti-symmetric with respect to the origin. It is useful to think of the Fourier series as a change of representation. Instead of representing the signal by the sequence of values specified by the original function $\ell(t)$, the same function is represented by the infinite sequence of coefficients $a_n$. (see figure: Two representations for the ramp function. (left) Time domain. (right) Fourier domain with coefficients of the sine series.) This representation is important for studying linear systems and convolutions.
concepts.motivation_md: Fourier series simplify the analysis of complex periodic signals by decomposing them into simple, fundamental oscillations, which are easier to manipulate in linear systems.
concepts.recap_md: - It decomposes periodic functions into an infinite sum of sine and cosine waves. - The series provides an alternative frequency-domain representation of a signal via its coefficients.

concepts.title: Sine Series
concepts.one_liner: A sine series is a Fourier expansion that represents a signal, such as a ramp, as an infinite sum of weighted sine functions.
concepts.content: A sine series is a type of Fourier expansion, such as the expansion of the ramp signal $\ell(t)=t/2$. Fourier showed that a ramp could be written as the following infinite sum: $$\frac{1}{2} t =  \sin (t) - \frac{1}{2}  \sin (2t) + \frac{1}{3} \sin (3t) - \frac{1}{4}  \sin (4t) + ...$$ The result of this series approximates the ramp with increasing accuracy as more terms are added. Adding higher frequency sines adds more details to the resulting function, making it closer to the ramp. (see figure: Reconstruction of a ramp with the first five sine functions.) These series reveal the periodic nature of the resulting function over larger intervals, such as $t \in (-4 \pi, 4 \pi)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Sine series are particularly useful for representing odd functions or functions defined on specific intervals, allowing for the approximation of complex shapes using simple harmonic components.

concepts.title: Campbell and Robson Chart
concepts.one_liner: The Campbell and Robson chart is a separable image used to experience the transfer function of the human visual system.
concepts.content: To experience the transfer function of our own visual system, we can construct an $N \times M$ image defined by: $$\ell\left[n,m\right] = A\left[m\right] \sin(2 \pi f\left[night] n/N)$$ with amplitude $A\left[might] = A_{min} \left(\frac{A_{max}}{A_{min}}\right)^{m/M}$ and frequency $f\left[night] = f_{min} \left(\frac{f_{max}}{f_{min}}ight)^{n/N}$. The amplitude varies from $A_{max}$ to $A_{min}$ on a logarithmic scale, while the frequency grows from $f_{min}=1$ up to $f_{max}=60$. concepts.title: Contrast Sensitivity Function (CSF)
concepts.one_liner: The contrast sensitivity function (CSF) describes the human visual system's sensitivity to different spatial frequencies, acting as a band-pass filter.
concepts.content: (see figure: Contrast sensitivity function shown by the Campbell and Robson chart. The image shows a sine wave of increasing frequency from left to right, and increasing amplitude from top to bottom. Can you...) Although the Campbell and Robson chart is mathematically separable, it is not perceived as such. Tracing the region where the sine wave seems to disappear reveals a curve known as the contrast sensitivity function (CSF). This curve shows that the visual system acts like a band-pass filter: it is sensitive to middle spatial frequencies (peaking around 6 cycles/degree) and less sensitive to very low and very high spatial frequencies. The CSF closely resembles the magnitude of the transfer function of the filter $H \left[ u,v \right]$ that approximates the human visual system.
concepts.motivation_md: The CSF characterizes the limits of human vision, explaining why we are better at seeing certain patterns and details than others based on their spatial frequency.

concepts.title: Locality of Fourier vs. Pixel Representations
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform provides information about what spatial frequencies are present in an image but lacks information about where they occur.
concepts.content: The Fourier transform has a major drawback as an image representation: it is too global. Every sinusoidal component covers the entire image. While the Fourier transform tells us what is happening in the image based on spatial frequency content, it tells us nothing about where it is happening. Conversely, a pixel representation provides great spatial localization, but a pixel value alone does not reveal much about the overall content. We seek a representation that lies between these two extremes.

concepts.title: Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) transforms a finite-sized image into a complex frequency-domain representation.
concepts.content:
The **Discrete Fourier Transform** (DFT) transforms an image $\ell\left[n,m ight]$, of finite size $N 	imes M$, into the complex image Fourier transform $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v ight]$ as: 

$$\mathscr{L}\left[u,v ight] = \mathcal{F} \left\{ \ell\left[n,m ight] ight\} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \, \ell\left[n,m ight] \exp{ \left( -2\pi j \left(  rac{u\, n}{N} +  rac{v\, m}{M} ight) ight)} $${#eq-fourier}

We call $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v ight]$ the Fourier transform of $\ell\left[m,n ight]$. The relationship between the signal and its transform is often represented as: 

$$\ell\left[n,m ight] \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \mathscr{L}\left[u,v ight]$$
concepts.motivation_md: The DFT allows us to analyze the frequency content of digital signals and images, enabling operations like filtering, compression, and feature extraction in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The DFT maps a spatial image $\ell[n,m]$ to a complex frequency-domain representation $\mathscr{L}[u,v]$.

concepts.title: Periodicity of the Discrete Fourier Transform
concepts.one_liner: The Discrete Fourier Transform and its inverse are periodic functions with periods determined by the dimensions of the image.
concepts.content: Since $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is obtained as a sum of complex exponentials with a common period of $N,M$ samples, the function $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is also periodic: $\mathscr{L}\left[u+aN,v+bM \right] = \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$. Similarly, the result of the inverse DFT is a periodic image. This can be verified from the inverse transform relation, showing that $\ell\left[n+aN,m+bM \right] = \ell\left[n,m \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding periodicity is crucial for correctly handling boundary conditions and avoiding artifacts like aliasing or wrap-around errors when processing images in the frequency domain.
concepts.recap_md: - Both the DFT and its inverse produce periodic functions with periods $N$ and $M$.

slots.example: Since $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is obtained as a sum of complex exponentials with a common period of $N,M$ samples, the function $\mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ is also periodic: $\mathscr{L}\left[u+aN,v+bM \right] = \mathscr{L}\left[u,v \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$. Similarly, the result of the inverse DFT is a periodic image. This can be verified from the inverse transform relation, showing that $\ell\left[n+aN,m+bM \right] = \ell\left[n,m \right]$ for any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$.

concepts.title: Centered Formulation of the DFT
concepts.one_liner: The centered formulation of the DFT shifts the zero-frequency component to the center of the frequency interval for better visualization.
concepts.motivation_md: Centering the zero frequency makes the spectrum easier to interpret visually, as low frequencies (the most important parts of most images) are grouped in the middle.
concepts.recap_md: - Centering the DFT places the DC component at the origin of the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
concepts.one_liner: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is an algorithm that efficiently computes the DFT by reducing computational complexity to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.content: The DFT became very popular thanks to the **Fast Fourier Transform** (FFT) algorithm. The most common FFT algorithm is the Cooley–Tukey algorithm, which reduces the computation cost from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Without the FFT, calculating Fourier transforms for large images or signals would be computationally prohibitive for real-time applications.
concepts.recap_md: - The FFT is a highly efficient algorithm for computing the Discrete Fourier Transform.

concepts.title: Least-Squares Reconstruction from Fourier Components
concepts.one_liner: Reconstructing an image from its largest Fourier components provides the optimal least-squares approximation for a given number of basis functions.
concepts.content: An image can be reconstructed from partial sums of its Fourier components. @fig-DFT_b shows partial sums of the Fourier components of an image. In each partial sum of $N$ components, we use the largest $N$ components of the Fourier transform. Using the fact that the Fourier basis functions are orthonormal, it is straightforward to show that this is the best least-squares reconstruction possible from each given number of Fourier basis components. The first image shows what is reconstructed from the largest Fourier component, which turns out to be $\mathscr{L}\left[0,0 \right]$. This component encodes the DC value of the image, therefore the resulting image is just a constant. The next two components correspond to two complex conjugates of a very slow varying wave. As more components get added, the figure slowly emerges. In this example, the first 127 coefficients are sufficient for recognizing this $64 \times 64$ resolution image.
concepts.motivation_md: This property explains why Fourier-based compression (like JPEG) is so effective: we can discard many small coefficients and still maintain a high-quality approximation of the original image.
concepts.recap_md: - Fourier basis functions are orthonormal, making partial sums optimal in a least-squares sense.
